shots.composition_notes: Static wide two-shot in an empty underground parking garage; both characters centered slightly left-of-center walking toward camera-right, full bodies in frame with generous headroom under the low ceiling pipes. Symmetrical rows of columns recede on both sides, reinforcing a deep, empty, sterile space. Episode title card ('PARKING LOT', 'Episode 3') is overlaid as text, not a physical camera move.

Locked-off medium shot framed through the silver elevator door track, which acts as a hard vertical crop on both sides of the frame like a secondary letterbox. The doors physically slide closed (going nearly black) and reopen within this single held camera position, so the doors' motion -- not the camera -- creates the only movement; the couple stands frozen in the exact same blocking (husband screen-left/background depth, wife screen-right/foreground) for the entire exchange, reinforcing the joke that time is passing without them moving.

Hard cut to an extreme close-up isolating only the husband's head and upper shoulders, centered and framed dead-on with his overlarge nose and glasses as the focal point; the wife is cropped out almost entirely except for a sliver of her shoulder/hair at the far right edge, visually sidelining her for the reaction beat. Background garage columns are thrown well out of focus, isolating the face against negative space.
Full-black end-card frame with centered gold serif title ('LOW BATTERY PEOPLE') and smaller white credit line ('CREATED BY NIN.') stacked beneath it; no scene geometry, pure static graphic card.

framing_patterns_notes: The scene consistently escalates from an open, static wide two-shot establishing the location to a static medium shot with an in-frame architectural crop (the elevator doors), then punches in to an extreme close-up on a single character's face for the payoff line -- each stage narrows the frame and isolates the characters further without ever using camera pans, tilts, or zooms; all movement in the video is blocking/prop movement (walking, doors sliding) rather than actual camera motion, and every shot is centrally composed and locked-off.
